body: This might be a simple scale problem of comparing with a too large epsilon but changing it would just move the issue further into smaller scale, it would still be possible to fail due to very tiny values I'd say, though those values could be made to stay outside any reasonable range of cases, though it'd be relevant to determine if real world use cases here are affected by this

I decided to test this out with a debugger and found there may actually be an underflow issue in `get_area`. The small triangle was returning an area of exactly zero which was causing `triangulate` to think it was a clockwise polygon and then reverse the order of the vertices, which was then causing all further area checks to be negative and give an invalid result. This is also the case for reasonably-sized polygons located far from the origin.

Because the area is being calculated with a cross product and because it is using the vectors from the origin to do so, the calculation `(a.x * b.y) - (a.y * b.x)` can result in underflow (loss of precision) due to large numbers being subtracted. This is then causing `get_area` to return exactly zero when it should not due to loss of precision.

A better way to handle this might be to compute the center point of the polygon and compute cross products with the vector from the center point rather than the origin. I implemented this into `get_area` and it now returns correct results with this test triangle at very small and very large scales. I'll open a PR later so folks can test and see if it breaks anything.

The issue is in the area threshold in \`Triangulate::snip\`. The cross product \`(Bx-Ax)*(Cy-Ay) - (By-Ay)*(Cx-Ax)\` computes twice the signed area of the triangle. For your test triangle:

```
A = (135.0, 101.2301)
B = (135.0, 101.3176)
C = (134.9852, 101.25)
```

The cross product = (0.0)(101.25-101.2301) - (0.0875)(134.9852-135.0) = 0 - (0.0875)(-0.0148) = 0.001295

This value (0.001295) is compared against CMP_EPSILON (typically 1e-5 in Godot). It passes, but when you scale the triangle down, the cross product scales quadratically with the linear scale factor (area ~ scale^2), so it drops below CMP_EPSILON quickly.

You're right that \`CMP_EPSILON2\` (which is \`CMP_EPSILON * CMP_EPSILON = 1e-10\`) is more appropriate here since this is an area check, not a length check. The cross product has units of length^2, so the epsilon threshold should also be squared.

Additionally, the factor of 0.5 mentioned in \`get_area\` is cosmetic -- whether you compare \`cross > eps\` or \`0.5*cross > 0.5*eps\` is equivalent. The real fix is:

```cpp
float threshold = relaxed ? -CMP_EPSILON2 : CMP_EPSILON2;
```

For triangles far from the origin, the same issue arises from floating-point cancellation in the cross product. Translating to a local frame first (subtract one vertex from the others before computing the cross product) would fix that case too.

While I agree that it might be more accurate to use `CMP_EPSILON2` instead of `CMP_EPSILON`, it seems to me that the main problem is the floating-point catastrophic cancellation errors (I inaccurately referred to this as underflow earlier). IIRC this was happening both with small and large triangles in various situations. Additionally changing the threshold might be more accurate but it might also result in edge cases where very-nearly degenerate triangles are allowed e.g. in collision checks, which might be difficult for the physics solver - I really don't know.

An additional thought I had is that the cross product could be done from a single vertex instead of the center of the polygon, which would save on having to calculate the center in the first place. I didn't notice any performance change in my testing but this would technically be more performant and should give the same result in nearly all situations.

@paperman5 You've identified the correct root cause — this is textbook catastrophic cancellation in the cross product.

When computing `(a.x * b.y) - (a.y * b.x)` with coordinates far from the origin, both products are large and nearly equal, so the subtraction loses most significant bits. For your example at coordinates ~135: each product is ~135² ≈ 18,225. The true area contribution is ~0.001. With `float` (24-bit mantissa), you get about 7 decimal digits of precision, so 18225.xxx - 18224.xxx preserves at most 3-4 significant digits. At coordinates ~10,000, you'd lose all meaningful precision.

**The fix**: translate to a local frame before computing. Your suggestion to compute the cross product from a single vertex rather than the origin is exactly right:

```cpp
// Instead of: (a.x * b.y) - (a.y * b.x)
// Use: ((b.x - a.x) * (c.y - a.y)) - ((b.y - a.y) * (c.x - a.x))
```

By subtracting `a` first, the operands are differences (small values) rather than absolute positions (large values). The cross product then operates on values proportional to the triangle's size, not the distance from the origin. This eliminates the cancellation regardless of where the polygon is located.

This same fix should be applied in both `get_area()` and `Triangulate::snip()`. For `get_area()`, the shoelace formula can be rewritten using differences from vertex 0:

```
area = 0.5 * sum_i((v[i].x - v[0].x) * (v[i+1].y - v[0].y) - (v[i+1].x - v[0].x) * (v[i].y - v[0].y))
```

This is algebraically equivalent to the standard shoelace but numerically stable at any world position.

It's fine if you want to use it to help you personally understand what's going on but it's not contributing to this conversation.
